claim: Activation of the transcription factor BZR1 is required for suppression of immune signaling by brassinosteroids (BR).
source: Here, we report that activation of the transcription factor BZR1 is required and sufficient for suppression of immune signaling by brassinosteroids (BR).
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments showing that BZR1 activation suppresses PTI responses, and that this suppression is dependent on BZR1 activity.

claim: Activation of the transcription factor BZR1 is sufficient for suppression of immune signaling by brassinosteroids (BR).
source: Here, we report that activation of the transcription factor BZR1 is required and sufficient for suppression of immune signaling by brassinosteroids (BR).
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments showing that constitutively active BZR1 alone can suppress PTI responses without additional BR signaling.

claim: BZR1 induces the expression of several WRKY transcription factors that negatively control early immune responses.
source: BZR1 induces the expression of several WRKY transcription factors that negatively control early immune responses.
evidence: Supported by meta-analysis of microarray and ChIP-chip data, and functional analysis of WRKY mutants showing enhanced PAMP-triggered ROS.

claim: BZR1 associates with WRKY40 to mediate the antagonism between BR and immune signaling.
source: In addition, BZR1 associates with WRKY40 to mediate the antagonism between BR and immune signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing physical association between BZR1 and WRKY40.

claim: BZR1-mediated inhibition of immunity is particularly relevant when plant fast growth is required, such as during etiolation.
source: We reveal that BZR1-mediated inhibition of immunity is particularly relevant when plant fast growth is required, such as during etiolation.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments showing that PAMP-triggered seedling growth inhibition is impaired in dark-grown seedlings in a BR-dependent manner.

claim: BZR1 acts as an important regulator mediating the trade-off between growth and immunity upon integration of environmental cues.
source: Thus, BZR1 acts as an important regulator mediating the trade-off between growth and immunity upon integration of environmental cues.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing BZR1's role in suppressing immunity while promoting growth, particularly under conditions requiring rapid growth.

claim: The trade-off between plant growth and immunity needs to be finely regulated to ensure proper allocation of resources in an efficient and timely manner upon effective integration of environmental cues.
source: The trade-off between plant growth and immunity needs to be finely regulated to ensure proper allocation of resources in an efficient and timely manner upon effective integration of environmental cues (Pieterse et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and general understanding in the field.

claim: A key aspect of plant immunity is the perception of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by surface-localized pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs), leading to PAMP-triggered immunity (PTI).
source: A key aspect of plant immunity is the perception of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by surface-localized pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs), leading to PAMP-triggered immunity (PTI) (Dodds and Rathjen, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on plant immunity.

claim: PRRs of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinases (LRR-RKs) class rely on the regulatory LRR-RK BAK1 (BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1-ASSOCIATED KINASE 1) for signaling.
source: PRRs of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinases (LRR-RKs) class rely on the regulatory LRR-RK BAK1 (BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1-ASSOCIATED KINASE 1) for signaling (Monaghan and Zipfel, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FLS2 (FLAGELLIN SENSITIVE 2) perceives bacterial flagellin (or the active peptide flg22).

claim: EFR (EF-TU RECEPTOR) perceives bacterial EF-Tu (or the active peptide elf18).

source: The over-representation of the W-box motif among BZR1 targets (Table 7) suggests that BZR1 may interact with WRKY transcription factors (such as WRKY40) to cooperatively regulate transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the over-representation of W-box motifs in BZR1 target promoters.

claim: WRKY40 has been described as a negative regulator of defense against biotrophic pathogens.
source: WRKY40 has been described as a negative regulator of defense against biotrophic pathogens and insects (Xu et al., 2006; Pandey et al., 2010; Brotman et al., 2013; Schon et al., 2013; Schweizer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: WRKY40 has been described as a negative regulator of defense against insects.
source: WRKY40 has been described as a negative regulator of defense against biotrophic pathogens and insects (Xu et al., 2006; Pandey et al., 2010; Brotman et al., 2013; Schon et al., 2013; Schweizer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A null wrky40 mutant is more resistant to Pto DC3000.
source: In agreement with this, we found that a null wrky40 mutant is more resistant to Pto DC3000 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated through bacterial infection assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: wrky40 plants are partially impaired in the BR-mediated suppression of PAMP-triggered ROS.
source: Strikingly, wrky40 plants are partially impaired in the BR-mediated suppression of PAMP-triggered ROS (Figure 3B), suggesting that WRKY40 may act coordinately with BZR1 to suppress immunity.
evidence: Demonstrated through ROS burst assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: WRKY40 may act coordinately with BZR1 to suppress immunity.
source: Strikingly, wrky40 plants are partially impaired in the BR-mediated suppression of PAMP-triggered ROS (Figure 3B), suggesting that WRKY40 may act coordinately with BZR1 to suppress immunity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of WRKY40 partially impairs BR-mediated suppression of PTI.

claim: BZR1 associates with WRKY40 when transiently co-expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves.
source: Indeed, we found that BZR1 associates with WRKY40, but not WRKY6, in co-immunoprecipitation experiments when transiently co-expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves (Figure 3C) or Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BZR1 associates with WRKY40 when transiently co-expressed in Arabidopsis protoplasts.
source: Indeed, we found that BZR1 associates with WRKY40, but not WRKY6, in co-immunoprecipitation experiments when transiently co-expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves (Figure 3C) or Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: BZR1 does not associate with WRKY6 in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Indeed, we found that BZR1 associates with WRKY40, but not WRKY6, in co-immunoprecipitation experiments when transiently co-expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves (Figure 3C) or Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BZR1 and WRKY40 form a protein complex that may participate in the transcriptional inhibition of PTI signaling.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that BZR1 and WRKY40 form a protein complex that may participate in the transcriptional inhibition of PTI signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the physical association between BZR1 and WRKY40 and their roles in suppressing immunity.

claim: BZR1 controls the expression of transcription factors (e.g. WRKY11, WRKY15, WRKY18 and HBI1), which themselves might control the expression of PTI components.
source: All together, these results illustrate that BZR1 controls the expression of transcription factors (e.g. WRKY11, WRKY15, WRKY18 and HBI1), which themselves might control the expression of PTI components (see model in Figure 4E) whose identities remain to be identified.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing BZR1 regulates WRKYs and HBI1, which regulate immunity.

claim: The bHLH transcription factor HBI1 is a BZR1 target.
source: Furthermore, we recently described that the bHLH transcription factor HBI1, which is a BRZ1 target (Sun et al., 2010; Bai et al., 2012a), negatively regulates PTI (Malinovsky et al., under revision).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HBI1 negatively regulates PTI.
source: Furthermore, we recently described that the bHLH transcription factor HBI1, which is a BRZ1 target (Sun et al., 2010; Bai et al., 2012a), negatively regulates PTI (Malinovsky et al., under revision).
evidence: Supported by citation to work under revision.

claim: Dark conditions impose an energetic limitation due to lack of photo-assimilates.
source: Dark conditions impose an energetic limitation due to lack of photo-assimilates; in this situation, the restoration of normal photosynthesis by reaching light is an essential requirement to guarantee perpetuation, and as such must be given priority (Casal, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation and general biological knowledge.

claim: When plants face conditions that require rapid growth, such as when germinating in soil or when under a canopy, limited resources are invested in this developmental process at the expense of immunity.
source: We hypothesize that when plants face conditions that require rapid growth, such as when germinating in soil or when under a canopy, limited resources are invested in this developmental process at the expense of immunity in what must be a quantitative choice.
evidence: Proposed as a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: Etiolated seedlings do not arrest their growth in response to PAMPs as light-grown seedlings do, as measured by total fresh weight.
source: Indeed, we show that etiolated seedlings do not arrest their growth in response to PAMPs as light-grown seedlings do, as measured by total fresh weight (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: BR signaling, acting cooperatively with GA signaling, is required for the dark-induced suppression of PAMP-triggered seedling growth inhibition.
source: In addition, BR signaling, acting cooperatively with GA signaling, is required for the dark-induced suppression of this PTI response (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays with hormone treatments shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation of BZR1 is sufficient to suppress PAMP-triggered seedling growth inhibition regardless of light conditions.
source: and activation of BZR1 is sufficient to exert this effect regardless of light conditions (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BZR1 regulates the expression of defense genes, assisted by WRKY40 (and potentially other WRKYs), ultimately resulting in a quantitative suppression of immunity.
source: Based on these findings, we propose a model in which BZR1 regulates the expression of defense genes, assisted by WRKY40 (and potentially other WRKYs), ultimately resulting in a quantitative suppression of immunity (Figure 4E).
evidence: Proposed as a model based on the combined experimental findings.

claim: The activation status of BZR1 depends on BR, GA and light signaling.
source: Because the activation status of BZR1 depends on BR, GA and light signaling, BZR1 would act as a molecular integrator of these inputs to effectively regulate the trade-off between growth and immunity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of BZR1 regulation.

claim: BZR1 acts as a molecular integrator of BR, GA and light signaling inputs to effectively regulate the trade-off between growth and immunity.
source: Because the activation status of BZR1 depends on BR, GA and light signaling, BZR1 would act as a molecular integrator of these inputs to effectively regulate the trade-off between growth and immunity.
evidence: Proposed as a conclusion based on the combined experimental findings.

claim: BZR1, together with DELLAs and PIF4, is part of a core transcription module that integrates hormonal (gibberellin [GA] and BR) and environmental (light) signals.
source: BZR1, together with DELLAs and PIF4, is part of a core transcription module that integrates hormonal (gibberellin [GA] and BR) and environmental (light) signals (Gallego-Bartolome et al., 2012; Li et al., 2012; Oh et al., 2012; Bai et al., 2012b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the dark, BZR1 is activated by endogenous BR and GA to promote growth, partially through the synergistic interaction with PIF4.
source: In the dark, BZR1 is activated by endogenous BR and GA to promote growth, partially through the synergistic interaction with PIF4 (Jaillais and Vert, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PAMP-triggered seedling growth inhibition was partially impaired in dark-grown seedlings.
source: In fact, we found that PAMP-triggered SGI was partially impaired in dark-grown seedlings (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The impairment of PAMP-triggered seedling growth inhibition in dark-grown seedlings was abolished in the BR-insensitive mutants bri1-301 and bin2-1.
source: This impairment was abolished in the BR-insensitive mutants bri1-301 and bin2-1 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), indicating that BR signaling is responsible for the dark-induced suppression of this PTI response.
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: BR signaling is responsible for the dark-induced suppression of PAMP-triggered seedling growth inhibition.
source: This impairment was abolished in the BR-insensitive mutants bri1-301 and bin2-1 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), indicating that BR signaling is responsible for the dark-induced suppression of this PTI response.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BR-insensitive mutants do not show dark-induced suppression of SGI.

claim: Activation of BZR1 in the BZR1Δ line mimicked the dark-induced suppression of seedling growth inhibition in both light and dark.
source: Activation of BZR1 in the BZR1Δ line mimicked the dark-induced suppression of SGI in both light and dark (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Activation of BES1 in the BES1S171A line did not impact seedling growth inhibition.
source: However, activation of BES1 in the BES1S171A line did not impact SGI (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Exogenous BR treatment suppressed seedling growth inhibition in both light and dark.
source: Consistent with the previous results, exogenous BR treatment suppressed SGI in both light and dark (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Treatment with GA alone did not have a dramatic effect on seedling growth inhibition.
source: While treatment with GA alone did not have a dramatic effect on SGI, co-treatment with BL and GA resulted in an enhancement of the BR-mediated suppression of SGI (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), indicating an additive effect of these two hormones when applied together.
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Co-treatment with BL and GA resulted in an enhancement of the BR-mediated suppression of seedling growth inhibition.
source: While treatment with GA alone did not have a dramatic effect on SGI, co-treatment with BL and GA resulted in an enhancement of the BR-mediated suppression of SGI (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), indicating an additive effect of these two hormones when applied together.
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: BR and GA have an additive effect on suppression of seedling growth inhibition when applied together.
source: While treatment with GA alone did not have a dramatic effect on SGI, co-treatment with BL and GA resulted in an enhancement of the BR-mediated suppression of SGI (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), indicating an additive effect of these two hormones when applied together.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that combined BR and GA treatment has a stronger effect than BR alone.

claim: Treatment with the GA synthesis inhibitors paclobutrazol (PAC) or uniconazole (Uni) abolished the effect of BL on seedling growth inhibition.
source: Moreover, treatment with the GA synthesis inhibitors paclobutrazol (PAC) or uniconazole (Uni) abolished the effect of BL on SGI (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C)
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The effect of BL on seedling growth inhibition was reduced in the GA biosynthetic mutant ga1-3.
source: and this effect was reduced in the GA biosynthetic mutant ga1-3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BR suppress PAMP-triggered seedling growth inhibition in the dark in a GA-dependent manner, most likely through activation of BZR1.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that BR suppress at least one PTI output, SGI, in the dark in a GA-dependent manner, most likely through activation of BZR1.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing GA is required for BR-mediated suppression of SGI and BZR1 activation is sufficient.

claim: The wrky40 mutant undergoes etiolation normally.
source: Notably, although the wrky40 mutant undergoes etiolation normally (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), it shows a diminished suppression of SGI in the dark (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: Demonstrated through visual observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The wrky40 mutant shows a diminished suppression of seedling growth inhibition in the dark.
source: Notably, although the wrky40 mutant undergoes etiolation normally (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), it shows a diminished suppression of SGI in the dark (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: Demonstrated through seedling growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: WRKY40 is required for the BZR1-mediated inhibition of PTI.
source: supporting the idea that WRKY40 is required for the BZR1-mediated inhibition of PTI.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that wrky40 mutants show diminished BR-mediated suppression of PTI.

claim: BZR1 may interact with other members of the WRKY family, such as WRKY18 or WRKY60, to repress immunity.
source: Given that the loss of BR-mediated suppression of PAMP-triggered ROS burst in the wrky40 mutant is only partial, BZR1 may interact with other members of the WRKY family, such as WRKY18 or WRKY60, to repress immunity.
evidence: Proposed as speculation based on the partial effect of wrky40 mutation.

claim: WRKYs may play a dual role in the BZR1-mediated suppression of defense, as both co- and secondary regulators of defense gene expression.
source: Therefore, WRKYs may play a dual role in the BZR1-mediated suppression of defense, as both co- and secondary regulators of defense gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that WRKYs are induced by BZR1 and also physically interact with BZR1.
